utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, legal assistants, court reporters, the registrar; good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. McCloskey, from the Prosecution. I see we have a new member of your team today; good morning. Good morning, Defence counsel, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic; good morning, General Krstic. We are going to resume our case. Good morning, madam. Can you hear me? I didn't hear an answer. Can you hear me? Yes, I'm in front of you. I'm talking to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Do you want me to read out loud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, please read it loudly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, please. Can you get a little closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphone be switched on as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a protected witness, Madam Registrar? Please look at that piece of paper to see simply whether your name is written on it, and tell us yes or no if that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please feel at ease. You are going to answer questions which, first, the Office of the Prosecutor is going to put to you. I see Mr. Harmon on his feet, so Mr. Harmon is going to question you. He is to your right, already on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, good morning, and good morning to my colleagues for the Defence. I will not be leading this witness. I wanted to take the opportunity to formally introduce my colleague, Ms. Magda Karagiannakas who will be leading the examination of this witness and the next witness. I thought it appropriate to formally introduce her since she is a new face in this courtroom. Now I pass the floor to Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. We welcome with pleasure Ms. Magda. I think this will be her first official address in the Tribunal, so I wish you welcome. You have the floor, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning to you and to the Defence. Examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what your nationality is and what your religion is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I am a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in a village in the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What level of education did you achieve at school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Four years of elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you proceed any further in your elementary schooling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: We didn't have the means, especially not for girls. Rather, boys were educated to a higher level if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the normal educational level for girls in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Well, so-so. Girls attended to the household and housework; they engaged in knitting and embroidering and farming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you when you got married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I was going on to 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it normal in your village for girls to get married at this age or an earlier age or at a later age, if at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: It was quite normal for girls to get married at that age; some at a slightly earlier age. But from 23 on, it was reckoned that she was a bit late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you got married, where did you go to live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I went to the place where I stayed until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away from Srebrenica town was this village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Not far. I don't know whether it was roughly half an hour on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many children you have and when they were born? But please don't tell me their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I had four children (redacted) (redacted), about the end of December. Then the second delivery was in 1981; actually, my third child, second delivery. I had my fourth child in 1986, on the 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had four children. Was it normal in your village to have large families or small families, or were there many people without any children at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Well, that was quite exceptional if people didn't have children at all because they couldn't, but it was normal to have four, five, even six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how your husband was employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: My husband worked in a company, transportation company called (redacted) [phoen] In Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: My husband sometimes stood in for the manager, and sometimes he worked as the boss in this company, as a kind of chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your job or role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: My role was to be a faithful housewife, to work hard, to take care of the household and its needs, to look after the children, to do the housework and the farming and the land, everything that was necessary. To tend the livestock, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who made the decisions in your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: My husband was head of the family and the household and everything, but we would consult if necessary and take decisions. If I were to suggest something, he wouldn't humiliate me; we would decide together. But he was the number one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who out of your family dealt with the authorities and any paperwork that you had to complete or your family needed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: That was all my husband's affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who out of your family managed the finances and the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: My husband earned the money and brought it home, and then together we would decide what we needed, what for, and how much, and we spent it like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the way in which your family was organised common or uncommon in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: It was very common. That is how it was in all the households. We were not in any way exceptional. That is how things were in our part of the country and in the village specifically. One had to know who was in charge, who was the head of the family, the head of the household and the property, so nothing could be done without him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they aware of the way in which your family and other Muslim families were organised in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Yes, they did know. We were friends, in fact. We went to have coffee at each other's houses. And if we were working on something, we would help one another. We would help them, and they would help us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for me your house, your land, and any livestock that you may have had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I can't really describe the land, I can just tell you that I had more than a hundred dulums, a dulums being 900 square metres. I'm not sure exactly how much, over a hundred, but I know that it was over a hundred. Then I had up to 50 sheep, about 15 goats, sometimes as many as a hundred chicken. My house was 10 by 12 metres, and it had a first floor. There was a separate entrance for the ground floor and a separate one for the first floor. Then the stable was about ten metres long. Next to the stable there was a garage. In the stable we held cows and horses. We had a separate stable for the sheep. Then we had a smoking shed for meat. Then we had a plum area, six by two and a half, an outside toilet next to the stable, then a chicken pen. That was separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general, how would you describe your standard of living at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: How can I describe it? It was a kind of life one could only hope for, the kind of life we had before the war. One had one's own land. You could produce what you wanted: vegetables, fruit, tend livestock, dairy products, everything. Whatever you needed, you had everything. My husband was working in a public company. He brought home his earnings. All we had to do was enjoy life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like to focus your attention on the events in Srebrenica in July 1995. At that time the attack on Srebrenica started, were you living with your husband and your sons in your home about three kilometres from Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the attack commenced, did you and your family leave your home to go into the woods because shells had fallen near your house and you feared for your safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Yes. We were sleeping that night. We knew that the UNPROFOR was there, and we felt safe. We were working and sleeping normally, even though they would shoot arbitrarily whenever they wanted because they were close by, when they would see people in the fields. So we were sleeping that night and early in the morning when the shelling started, we were so scared, we jumped up. A shell fell close to our house. The windows shattered. The whole house shook. There was so much dust that we could hardly see one another through it. Then we started screaming. The children jumped up in their underwear, in their T-shirts. They started screaming. My husband threw one by one of us out of the house to the right. There was a bit of shelter there, and he said run into the vale that was below the house to take shelter. And he helped one child after another get out of the house, and then me. I was screaming. I grabbed him; I didn't want to go without him. He said, "You go and I will follow." I turned around. There was a line with clothes hanging out to dry. I grabbed some things because the children had nothing on. And so we ran through our own fields that were sown with wheat and maize, and we ran and ran and the shells kept falling. When a child would trip in the wheat or corn, I would scream thinking he had been hit, but it was all right; they got up again. And we got to the bottom of this creek, and then we sought shelter in some kind of cellars and dugouts, but there were a lot of people there, so there wasn't enough room. There were others that had got there before us. And it was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after a few days, did you and your family subsequently go to Srebrenica town, to an UNPROFOR checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: We did. We were in the woods and along the streams for two or three days. Then we got to Srebrenica. Because I had a lot of relatives there who had been chased out of their homes earlier on, so I stayed with them for awhile, hoping that Srebrenica would be protected by the people who were protecting us. When we saw that nothing would come of it, people started moving towards UNPROFOR, where they were stationed. It's Vezionica or something; that is what the name of the area was where UNPROFOR was stationed. We all ran to them. You would think the whole world was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were at the checkpoint, did your husband and older son leave you to try and escape Srebrenica through the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Everyone was there. Men, women, children, all the young people. I remember very well it was Tuesday. We were hoping, and I'm still hoping, but we didn't know what was happening. People were crying, screaming. Shots could be heard all the time. Somebody was trying to comfort us, telling us, "Srebrenica will not fall. Don't take it too hard. Don't panic," but nothing came of it. They had some kind of makeshift radios; they were trying to listen to the news. People were hoping that something would happen. Then one could hear, for example, "We heard it on the radio. They will send the aeroplanes now. They will save us now." I remember very well that somebody had a very small radio set, but it was very unclear, everything I heard. At one point I heard that the situation in Srebrenica was calming down and that people were going back to their homes. But then I realised that nothing good would come of it because everybody had gathered around the UNPROFOR base. People had started gathering there two or three days before. They were all over the place, along the creeks, in the woods, hiding in the rocks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that the place that your husband and your older son left you to go to try and escape through the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: At that point, the shelling started again. The detonations were so loud, one would think that the whole earth was on fire. Somebody shouted out, "Nobody is ever going to come and save us." I remember some people saying, "Let us go through the woods," and "The adult men should go through the woods and women and children to UNPROFOR." At that point I told my husband for the last time, "We're not going to separate ourselves," and he told me not to worry. He told me to take two of our children and leave, and he said that he would join other men. But as we were talking, we could see that the shells were falling around the UNPROFOR base and women and children were being hit and wounded. Shells were falling on the building where people were staying. It was such a chaos. So we parted; my husband left with my eldest son. Then I realised that some Dutch soldiers were going towards the building we called Vezionica, and they were motioning to us to follow them. Then I thought, thank God they are going to save us. They're calling us to join them, and I was so sorry that my husband and son had left, that they had gone to the other side, thinking that the soldiers would protect us. So we followed them and we followed them in the direction of Potocari. On the way to Potocari, and we were walking all the time, the shells kept falling around us. Shots could be heard from all kinds of weapons, I don't know which ones, but we kept walking. The trucks with wounded people and other people that had boarded them were catching up with us. That is how we managed to reach Potocari, where there was a large number of old trucks and buses. I think that the temperature was around 37 or 38 degrees centigrade, and we took shelter behind the trucks. We were looking for some shade and water but there was no water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it true to say that you spent two nights in Potocari out in the open with your sons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: It was on Tuesday. On that day, we spent the evening there, the whole day Wednesday, and we were still there on Wednesday evening. Then there was this black Thursday that came. I remember it was around 10.00 or half past ten. We were still there, and at that time we reached the line near the trucks where people were waiting to be transported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Could I please have a glass of water? Things were getting worse and more horrible every day, every hour. We spent sometime there on that day, but we didn't have anything to eat, we didn't have any water to drink. We were looking for shelter and water all the time, and that is how we spent that first day. When the night fell finally --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: -- we were looking for a place to shelter ourselves. Yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned black Thursday. What happened on that black Thursday when you were going to be transported out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I was going to tell you the whole story from Tuesday to Thursday. Can I do that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the Judges have already heard quite a lot of evidence in this case about the events in Potocari, so for the purposes of my examination, I'm not going to ask you questions about those days. The Judges and the Defence may want to ask you questions about what happened on those days, and you should answer those questions if they ask them, but now I'd like you to focus your attention on the day that you were going to be transported out of Potocari, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Okay. So when that black Thursday came, it was in the early morning hours, and my child was still sleeping, the child that was about to be snatched from me. So I woke him up, telling him that we should leave, that we should go to the trucks. He got up. He wanted to eat -- I asked him if he wanted to eat something but he couldn't take anything. He complained about being dirty. He had some kind of white shirt on him. I took off that shirt and then I cleaned him a little bit. I had some other clothes in my bag and I gave it to him. I was trying to calm him down. I told him that we would soon be transported to some place where we could have a shower and wash ourselves a little bit. Then we moved closer to the line. There was a kind of tape around the area. There were a lot of people. We couldn't cross over. I realised that my son was not feeling well, that he was about to faint. Then I started looking for some water but there was no water anywhere. There was a friend of ours there, an elderly man, and he said that he would go and get some water for my son. So he left, and then after he came back he was totally white in his face. His wife was there. But he kept shaking his head like this and he was telling his wife something about some horrible things that he had seen. His wife wanted to know what he had actually seen, but he kept crying and shaking his head. He said, "I saw everything. I saw heads and limbs all over the place where I went to fetch some water." At that point my child started trembling, and he was about to faint again. Finally, it was our turn to approach the rope and we were finally let through. I felt relieved. I thought to myself, thank God. After everything I had seen, after I had seen people being separated, I kept thanking God because we seemed to have passed through, me, my children, and these friends of ours. But then there was a line of their soldiers standing there on both sides, on our left-hand side and on our right-hand side, and it was a kind of column that they had formed, a kind of gauntlet, a corridor that we had to pass through. We couldn't see the trucks or the buses. We had covered a distance of about 100 metres but we still couldn't see any vehicles. When we were halfway through, I heard a voice say, "Popovic, look out for this one," and I immediately realised that he was referring to my child. But then there were other children there as well. There was my sister-in-law's child and some other people. Then the soldiers insisted and I felt paralysed at one point. But I mustered some courage to whisper in my son's ear and to tell him, "Don't worry, sonny. Just go. Keep going." We walked for about 50 metres, and then from the left column one of their soldiers jumped out, and he spoke to my child. He told us to move to the right side, and he told my son, "Young man, you should go to the left side." And then he said, "Why me? I was born in 1981." But he repeated what he had said, "You people should go to the right-hand side." He had some kind of bags in his hand, and the soldier told him to throw the bag to the right side and to go to the left, but I grabbed him by his hand and I -- he kept repeating, "I was born in 1981. What will you do with me? What do you want me do?" And then I begged them, I pleaded with them. Why are you taking him? He was born in 1981. But he repeated his order. And I held him so hard, but he grabbed him. And then my son threw out that bag, and the soldier picked up the bag and threw it on a pile on the right-hand side, and he took my son's hand, and he dragged him to the left side. And he turned around, and then he told me, "Mommy, please, can you get that bag for me? Could you please get it for me?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, please, take your time. Take your time to calm down. We are here with you; we're listening to you. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: That was the last time I heard his voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take your time, madam. Do you think you'll need a break? Would you prefer to go on? If you feel able to continue, please let us know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can continue. My other child who was with me kept screaming. This child was born in 1986. He grabbed me by my hair; he was pulling my hair. He was shouting and screaming, "Mommy, they have taken my brother away. They have taken our brother." And then I was thinking about taking this other child and going to where my son had been taken, but he kept screaming. He was asking for his aunt that had been with us, but I just stood there thinking what to do. But he kept screaming, pulling my clothes, my hair, and then I started comforting him, and I told him to calm down. I was trying to tell him that his brother would not be harmed in any way. And I just stood there for a while. I didn't know what to do. I didn't know where to go. But at that point my sister-in-law came and her sister-in-law, and they took me with them. They told me to go with them, and we went to a truck. It was a large truck. It didn't have any canvas on. So they put me onto that truck, and we sat down. The truck was still standing, and I kept looking at that direction where they had taken him to. There was a bus full of men that was standing there, and there was some men around the bus as well. They were actually many of them. They could have been put in five more buses. And I was thinking, well, thank God, at least they have buses. They will be taken somewhere by a bus. But at that point our truck left, and I didn't see him again. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you then transported by that truck with your young son to Tisca where you got off and then walked to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Yes, but on the road to Tisca we were stoned on several occasions because it was an open truck which did not have any cover, any tarpaulin, and my other child was hit on his head. I had a kind -- some kind of shoes with me, and then I put them on my child's head. That happened the first time when we were stoned. But that happened once again, and a woman who was on the truck had a kind of a blanket, and I put the blanket on my child's head, and I put the shoes on my head. And this is how we were transported to this place which I didn't know. I didn't know what kind of place it was, what kind of town, but at one point the truck stopped, and we were told that we were in Tisca. And they told us that we would be taken from there to Kladanj. So we started getting off the truck. It was a rather high truck, and it was not very easy to get off the truck. I needed some help, and people helped me get down. There was a very big Cetnik standing there together with another one, a very young man, young boy who was actually smaller than my son who was born in 1986, but he was holding a rifle. And he told us to move on quickly. He told us "Hurry up, hurry up. Get off the truck." We kept quiet. We got off the truck, all of us. And we continued along the road on foot where they told us we should go in the direction of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will need to go into closed session for the next couple of questions I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will go into closed session -- or, rather, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to ask you some questions about life after the fall of Srebrenica. Can you describe where you live now and the type of accommodation it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I'm now living in a collective centre. You can only imagine what it's like. Every minute of the day I wish I was no longer alive. Some people singing, some people listening to music, another one dancing; everyone is doing whatever they like. My room is about four by six, something like that. That is where we sleep, where we live, where we cook. The bathroom, toilet, everything, all in one. That is where we have to dry our clothes and to have visitors. That's all we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you live with in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I'm living in that room with my son, born in 1986. I also have a daughter who has no accommodation at all. She comes to see me. She has two children of her own. So you can't keep it tidy. If you're in pyjamas, you can't change. You often sleep in the clothes you wear during the day. And that is how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you receive an income?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: I receive something based on my husband's employment in the company, and then out of his social insurance, I'm given an allowance, taking into account that I have a minor with me. But I'm not old enough to have a pension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much money do you receive a month?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 140 what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: Money. What do they call them? Marks, coupons. I don't know. These convertible marks or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you compare your standard of living today to the standard of living you had before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: There's no comparison. I've told you my whole life, what it was like before and what it is like now. How can you compare the two?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what has been the impact of these crimes on you and your son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: You can imagine what it has been. My young son, born in 1986, he has demands. He wants this and that, and he starts trembling when I tell him I don't have it, I can't afford it. Then he accuses me of all kinds of things, saying that it was my fault that things are like this. "If I had a father, he would give me everything." So you can imagine in addition to all my stress and anxieties, I have to try and console him. He keeps blaming me. "Perhaps it would have been better if you didn't have me even." And then sometimes I also think it would be better if none of us had survived. I would prefer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you feel about returning to your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: What would you suggest to me, after everything I've been through? If I had felt well and if I had strength. When war criminals are still walking around and doing what they want, what's the point about thinking -- even though I sometimes think that it would be better if we hadn't survived. Should I take him over there too to be killed and slaughtered? It's true that I loved my village and estate, but of course there's no comparison with the love one has for children. I did love it all, the house and the farm and everything, but what's the point of it all now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think has happened to your husband and your two sons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD
utterances.text: How do I know? As a mother, I still have hope. I just can't believe that this is true. How is it possible that a human being could do something like this, could destroy everything, could kill so many people? Just imagine this youngest boy I had, those little hands of his, how could they be dead? I imagine those hands picking strawberries, reading books, going to school, going on excursions. Every morning I wake up, I cover my eyes not to look at other children going to school, and husbands going to work, holding hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I won't ask any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, for the moment the Prosecutor has no further questions. Would you like to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever you say. I will tell you everything I know, whatever you ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We know that you are a very brave woman, but we're going to have a break because we normally have a break, and after that we'll come back here and we will continue to listen to you. For the moment, we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, have you had a little rest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now, madam -- I was saying, madam, that you are now going to answer questions which Defence counsel is going to put to you. I have already told you that you are a very brave woman, so now you're going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. No additional questions. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. President. Good morning, madam. Can you hear me? I am in front of you.

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I share the views of the president in saying that we have a great deal of admiration for your courage, and we understand and feel for your pain, but there is a life ahead of you, and the whole world is on your side. I simply wanted to ask you whether your husband before being arrested, whether he took part in any resistance or whether he attacked people on the other side? Was there any reason for his arrest in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were any weapons found in your home?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any political activity he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he selected among others, or did they round up people without any discrimination?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: One and all, as I just said, regardless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for your son, was he chosen among many other boys? Did they take a lot of other boys of his age?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: All the others, whoever was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say all of them, of what age were they? How old were they, the others, your son's friends?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Well, it depended. Some were younger than my son, a year or two. Some were a little older. There were men of different ages there. There were even babies that were being born. They took them, too, if they were boys, not to mention the older boys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but your son was born in 1981?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was 12, 13, 14?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: He was going on 14 then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he big? Did he look like a mature young man, in your opinion? Could one think that he was older?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: The children were snatched away. The children were quite tall because I was quite big and so was my husband, so they were not underdeveloped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you told them that he was born in 1981?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you returned to your house?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No. How can I go back? When we went to observe the 5th anniversary of this greatest massacre, I think the whole world was watching how they react, even today how they rally, the Cetniks, how they threaten and how they demonstrate their threats, and the security was such that we only just somehow managed to get through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you go back to see your house?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No. That day and the next day and the day after, after we had fled our houses towards Srebrenica to hide, we heard from some neighbours and friends who went back during the night to get some food that everything out there had been set on fire and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you still have any relationships with your former Serb neighbours? Have you picked up those relationships, or are you completely separate now?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: I have no contact. I never saw them again. I did recognise a neighbour when they took my child away from me, and I was watching out for them. I wanted to find them to ask them because I was hoping that perhaps he might have saved my son, because we were so close with all of our neighbours, not just them. But he was the only one I noticed there, and I hoped and prayed to find him, but I never managed to get in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have your neighbours changed their attitude towards you, or do they still have friendly feelings towards you? I'm talking about your Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: You mean up to the time they took my child? You mean the neighbour I recognised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the others.

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: I noticed him, and I saw that he could recognise me, too, because he cast a quick glance at me. We exchanged glances, and I thought that I should scream out for him to save my child, but then I thought better of it because I had heard from others that the neighbours were doing the worst things and so I thought maybe my child would fair even worse, so I restrained from addressing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And so you have no Serb neighbours around you; you don't visit one another at all?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Probably there are some, but I have no contact with them. Simply, we don't communicate. How do I know? I just can't believe that having the kind of life we had, that this could have happened, so I keep wondering. I don't know what to say to you, starting from myself and my children and onwards, further afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if you could remember, before this happened, did you hear any talk of a plan of what was going to happen, or were you completely taken by surprise? In the media, on the radio, et cetera, were there any announcements as to what would happen? Were there any threats?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No. They worked together in various companies, their men and our men, the men in our neighbours' families. Our children went to school together. We had land next to one another. When he had to collect the hay, and if it was going to rain, we would help them to do it quickly, and they would help us to collect the hay. So you couldn't notice anything at all until we saw that they were loading their families into trucks and cars, with supplies, and driving them away somewhere. I don't know where. Then someone asked, "Where are you going? What's happening?" and then their answer was very vague. "Some fools could come along and do who knows what. Of course, we won't hurt you and you won't hurt us, we believe that, but some fools may come along." So they thought it would be better to move for awhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They left a long time before those events, so they knew what was going to happen. How long beforehand did this happen?

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Not long before that happened. They didn't leave much earlier. I forgot what I was going to say a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never mind. I'm not asking you for dates. The point is they left before.

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: Yes. It was only after all these things happened that we thought about the reasons why they had left. Because they gave different answers; some people said they were going to stay with relatives in Serbia, to do some kind of work there; others were saying they were going on holiday. They were giving different answers. Only after all this happened, we realised why they had left and where they had left to, their families and their children. But the men stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you understood that they left in a collective manner; all the Serb families left together.

utterances.speaker: [Interpretation]  Yes.
utterances.text: No, we didn't really see them go together. But there were fields that belonged to them a little further away. Then some people would leave on one day and others on another day, and then somebody would say, "I saw that family leave," and then the next day, someone would say, "I saw this other family leave." And we were wondering. Until then, they didn't do anything wrong. They didn't hurt us and, of course, we didn't hurt them either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam. I wish you courage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have no questions for the witness except to thank you for coming and sharing your very sad story with the Tribunal. I think it will help us in making our decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me too, madam, I have a very small question for you. Do you have anything that you would like to say and that has not been asked of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I wanted to say if I had known these people would betray us the way they did, those who had sworn to protect us and signed documents to that effect, I would have saved my family, my husband and my children. We could have sought shelter somewhere and at least we would have died together and our bones would be together. I would have stayed in front of our house together with my whole family and let them all kill us together if I had known what would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, madam, I wish to repeat that you are an extremely brave woman. You have said that the body lives, but perhaps the soul needs to gain strength from the little hands of your son. You must continue living, at least if for no other reason than to testify about all those events that you have shared with us and to avoid, as you have said, that fools may appear again in the future. So that is a very good reason to continue living. We thank you very much for coming here and we would like to wish a better life for you and for all your loved ones. So you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say one more thing, please? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to appeal to you to ask Mr. Krstic, if you can, whether there is any hope for at least that little child that they snatched away from me, because I keep dreaming about him. I dream of him bringing flowers and saying, "Mother, I've come." I hug him and say, "Where have you been, my son?" and he says, "I've been in Vlasenica all this time." So I beg you, if Mr. Krstic knows anything about it, about him surviving some place ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, madam, I think all of us have heard your plea, and I think that all the people who are here and who can do something will do it. But I repeat, you have good reasons to continue living. All the people here present and all those listening to us will do whatever is possible to do. We understand and feel for your suffering. I will ask the usher to lead you out now. Thank you once again for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Magda.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have our next witness here ready to give testimony, and there are no protective measures in relation to this witness. Her name is Jasna Zecevic. We'd like her to be brought in, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. So we are now waiting for our next witness to be brought in. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I just wanted to say for the record that this witness that just left is pseudonym DD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Zecevic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now. Make yourself comfortable. Could you perhaps come a little closer to the microphone so that we can hear you better. Ms. Zecevic, you will first be answering questions that will be put to you by Ms. Magda Karagiannakas. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me your name and spell your last name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Jasna Zecevic, so last name is Z-e-c-e-v-i-c. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. Before we get started, I'd just like to remind you that we are both speaking the same language, but what we say has to be translated simultaneously into French and B/C/S, so that means that after I ask a question, I'd like you to talk a pause, a few minutes -- a minute or two break before you answer it. And I will do the same after you finish so that we give enough time for the translators to do their work. What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My nationality is I'm born in Croatia, and my father is from Bosnia, my mother is from Croatia, so we call it now "other." So my nationality is "other."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you currently live and how long have you been living there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm living now in Tuzla in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm living there for 30 [sic] years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, you said your nationality is "other"?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What's it mean, "other"?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It means that I don't have clear nationality because I live in Bosnia, and I'm not born in Bosnia, and I am a child of mixed marriage, so my father is Muslim, my mother is a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they call you "others"?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the term. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The term?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have different nationality in Bosnia now, and there is some people who are not -- it's not Bosnian nationality because we don't have still Bosnian nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in your passport is written "other"?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's nothing. Nothing is written. It is Bosnian passport is nationality. I'm living in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you have the Bosnian nationality?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bosnian nationality, but it's not existing Bosnian nationality. I mean, that's a special term we use in Bosnia. You can be in Bosnia a Serb, Croat, or Muslim, and "others."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And others are mixed marriages only, or foreigners?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mixed marriages and foreigners and everyone who are not Croat, Muslim, or Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They're called "others"?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, called "others".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is the term "other" a term used in the census forms to describe people that are not Bosnian -- or sorry, Muslim, Croatian, or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what are your academic qualifications?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I finished -- I'm an engineer of geology. I finish in 1989 on the faculty of Tuzla, mining and geology, and in 1991 I finished post-graduate study in geochemistry, also in the faculty of Tuzla, University of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you currently employed and what is your position?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Currently I'm working in NGO at an organisation Vive Zene. It's a non-government organisation. Vive Zene what means "woman alive," and I'm director of that NGO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the aim of your NGO, and how was it established?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So Vive Zene established in 1994 and established and with aim to provide the psycho-social support for the victim of war, to the women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is your organisation funded?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My organisation is funded from European Community, with the donation from European Community, from Netherlands government, Switzerland government, some other NGOs from Netherland and from Switzerland, from Sweden also, and England.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of programmes does Vive Zene run?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we have one programme of psycho-social support which we implement in a different settings. We implement the psycho-social programme in the residential part. We call it psycho-therapy centre for women and children traumatised by the war. And also in the community work, the same programme, and on the ambulant way so that outpatient are coming from time to time to the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your organisation work in collective centres and refugee towns and --

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we call community work. So our multidisciplinary team are working in the refugee settlements outside of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a multidisciplinary team. What is that team made up of or who is that team made up of?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Multidisciplinary team is consisting two therapists for the women, psychotherapists for the women, two psychotherapists for the children, two pedagogues who are working also with the children, three social worker, and one physiotherapist. That's -- we call it body therapist because she's working on a different way than usually physiotherapy. And the one doctor and one nurse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people has Vive Zene provided therapy for since its beginnings?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From 1994 until January 2000, we provide all our service in stationary part for 124 women and 222 children, that is a residential part; and around 4.011 women in ambulant way and 28 children, but these 28 children is just who attend on a psychotherapy programme; and there is more than 400 children what we treat in our pedagogical workshop in the community, in the refugee community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify a point, was it 411 women or 4.011 women that you provide ambulance service for?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people that you have treated, how many of them come from the Srebrenica survivor community, and by that I mean people that came from Srebrenica after the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that is in this number of stationary, what we treated in stationary concept, in stationary part, is 60 women from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you provided any ambulance services to these women?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this number what I said for ambulant is 180 women and from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What functions do you perform in your organisation now?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At this moment as a director of the centre, I am responsible for organising the life in the centre, organisational part, for the fund raising, for public relation, contact with the donors and assisting the women to organise their life inside the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that last task involve?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The last task we consider very important because the women who are living in the centre, as they are traumatised, so they don't have this internal structure with what we consider the normal life, so we are trying, I am trying, to give them support in organising very normal and simple things, like cleaning the house, taking care about their children, so that they have to have back this feeling of normal. Certain time for the breakfast, certain time for the lunch, so some rules to keep them in a normal structure. We are trying to give them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other experiences have you had with the Srebrenica community?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So with the Srebrenica community before the war I had also some experience because I worked for one month in mining -- my study was in Srebrenica. So with the Srebrenica community I could describe or I can tell my experience of very calm and nice community with some patriarchal structure in their community, and after the war I have different experience because working and living with these women who came after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you working and living with these women after the fall of Srebrenica, and by that I mean in what capacity? What were you doing for them?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So I already told you about this helping and assisting them. During that time they are living in our centre, to assist them, to give them back the strength that they can continue as much as is possible the normal life, and to be the family again. I mean, they are not complete family, but they are, because they have children. So it's very hard for them to understand that without the husband and without the men, they are the family with their children. So that is the main task what we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before you were director of Vive Zene, did you work for them in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before I become director, from 1996 I am director of Vive Zene, so I was working in Vive Zene from 1994 as translator with the psychologist from Germany, and she was treating the women traumatised by the war, and I was translator in psychotherapy in the group and individual treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that capacity, did you have any special contact with the women of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you were a translator, what sort of -- did you have -- what was your first contact with women from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First contact -- sorry, first contact with women from Srebrenica from 1995, it was in airport Dubrave when they came in July when they came from Srebrenica, as translator with these women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Had the survivors from the Srebrenica community in 1995 treated by your organisation come primarily from Srebrenica town or from the rural area surrounding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All of them we treat from 1995, they are coming from around Srebrenica, from the rural area. So they are not from the town of Srebrenica. But in that moment when they were from the town of Srebrenica, that was the second time that they were refugees. When they came to Tuzla, that was the second time. The first time they came in Srebrenica from their villages, I think from 1993. So they lived for two years in this enclave, protected enclave, and in 1995 they came as refugees again to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your experience and contact with the women and children from this survivor group, can you describe the respective roles of women and men in their society?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the society of Eastern Bosnia, or I can say that in the villages in Bosnia not just in Srebrenica, I can describe it as a traditional patriarchal family structure. So the point was that men were responsible for the family, so he was the one who made decisions, the decision-maker. He was working outside of the house, I mean public -- he was responsible for the public work; he earned the money. And the woman was responsible and worked in the house more and in the field. So she was responsible for the children but she didn't make the decisions. So that was common not just in the Srebrenica population but also in other villages in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, from your experience and contact with this survivor group, can you describe the way in which the people living in the rural areas surrounding Srebrenica supported themselves?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Their income, what they got, it was from the work the men had in mining companies, because usually they work in the mining companies and the factories around Srebrenica. And the field they had belonged to them. I mean, the field -- they had houses, and the field they were working, and they produced the food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How important would you say that a house and land was to the people from this survivor community?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Their house and their land was everything that they had, so that was their life. That's, for them, everything and only what they get -- what they have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, was the societal structure and the respective roles of men and women in this society common and widely known in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was very well known and very clarified and divided, who is the man and who is the woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to the issue of -- more specifically, how the Srebrenica survivor community that you have dealt with lives after the fall of Srebrenica. First of all, the issue of accommodation. What type of accommodation do survivors generally live in?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, at this moment, and after the fall of Srebrenica, they are living in collective settlements, refugee settlements, and so-called private accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a collective settlement?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A collective or refugee settlement is supposed to be the place for living for the people who are refugees from Eastern Bosnia or whatever, and those are the houses made by internationals -- the International Community. With four or five rooms in one house, it is supposed that one or two families live there but there are usually five or six families; so 20 people in one smaller house are living. They have a joint kitchen and a joint toilet. So they have in one room a few generations, maybe mother-in-law or mother, or mother and child, so a few generations are living in one room. They sleep there, they cook, they eat, they wash, they do everything in that small room. They live in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the refugees that live in these collective settlements own their houses or their apartments or their rooms?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who owns those rooms?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It belongs to the Bosnian country, I mean, to the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many victims from the fall of Srebrenica are living in the Tuzla municipality today?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the Tuzla municipality, it is around 7.000 refugees from Srebrenica from 1995. But altogether it's 140.000 refugees in the Tuzla surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in June of this year, you visited a collective centre with an investigator from the OTP who took a tape of your visit. I would now like to show you an excerpt of this video which I have previously shown you in my office, and I'd like you to comment on it after the end of the video, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could Exhibit 386 please be played, and if we could dim the lights as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which collective settlement is depicted in that video?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Spionica settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many collective centres are there in the Tuzla area which Srebrenica survivors live in?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is altogether eight collective settlements, and Srebrenica survivors are living in each. So they are divided in each settlement, but mostly they are living in three: Spionica, Nihatovici, and Karaula. They are in each settlement. They are not divided, separate from the other refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those conditions which you have described and which we have now seen in the video, in Spionica, are they typical of what one might expect to see?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This, what you see, is one of the nicer - we call it nicer - settlements, and this, what you see, it is in the summer so it is very clean. After action we had, we were doing the cleaning of the settlement, together with the people who are living there. So there are others, like Mrdici - we don't have it; I didn't see that - but Mrdici is on the top, on the surface of the former mining company. So during the summer you can't come with a car on top of that hill. This settlement, what we see, Spionica, during the winter, you saw the road, so it's very wet and you can't walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 390.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the exhibit from there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that a photo of?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the same settlement you see, Spionica, just in a different time. You see the children that are usually outside of the houses because they don't have any other place -- there is no infrastructure for normal life in such a settlement. So they are outside most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a playground in this settlement?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the playground, what you see, if you can call it a playground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you generally describe the lifestyle of the Srebrenica survivors who live in these settlements, in these collective centres?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The lifestyle? I will not call it a lifestyle because there is no life in this settlement. So they are living in, you saw, the small, small rooms. They don't have any individuality, so they don't have any normal conditions for the -- especially for the children to grow up in such a settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do the Srebrenica survivors that live in these settlements view them? Do they see them as permanent or temporary? Do they view them as their own?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is a big problem because they see it just as temporary, and they are living there for five years and they still feel that it's just temporary. So they don't do anything. As you can see on this picture, they don't do anything around their houses. Even if they used to work in their former life - we call it former life - around the garden to help the flowers like all other people, to have a nice garden, but because of this situation which they are in now, they are living in a so-called temporary, they are stuck in that, so they don't do anything for what we consider a normal life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that some Srebrenica survivors live in empty Serb houses. What is this accommodation generally like?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Generally, this accommodation in empty Serb houses is more or less the same as the collective settlements. They are also in one room. The government, they give them these places because there was no other places, there is not enough settlements. But they are maybe in a worse situation because they are split. These houses are not like this, together in one small community. So they are also isolated, more isolated than these people in the group. They are isolated in the settlement and they are individually isolated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the people living there own those houses or have any right to them?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, they don't have any rights. That is just temporary. They live just temporary because they have to go back one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Srebrenica survivor community that you and your organisation have dealt with, how many of them are employed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The women we treat, there is just one woman employed and she was employed after she finished some courses. It's not real employment. I mean, she's cleaning the houses around, the flats, so she earns some money for her children. But generally there is no employment between the women. They are not employed. Not just the refugees. I mean the situation in Bosnia, as you know, it's very hard to be employed at this moment. Not just because they are refugees, but they are not employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from what source, if any, do they receive any income?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the income, if they're lucky, they could get from the government, it's 300 Deutschemarks for the missing person. That's only what is officially allowed, 300 Deutschemarks, for one women and two or three children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do the survivor families have to pay from this 300 Deutschemarks a month?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this moment, they have to pay everything, the food, the clothes, everything that they need for the life of their children, to feed their children, to feed themselves, to pay -- they have some bonus for electricity that they don't have to pay in the collective settlements, and everything after that, they have to pay. But it's usually not less -- not so much. And also they have to buy wood or oven or dishes, everything that you need to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What standard of living would you say this income affords these people?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is no standard. I can't talk about the standard in this condition. It is just that they have to survive somehow so they are surviving. There is no life standard in such a condition so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to another issue, and that is the bureaucratic and social status of the Srebrenica survivors. What bureaucratic status do the Srebrenica survival women have?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Srebrenica women from 1995, they have now special status of missing -- they have missing husbands. That's new in our society. I mean, new for them, because in our society, it's very important that you have some status, especially as a woman. You have to be either divorced or married or to have clear status, but this is -- with missing husband, there is no status. So they are -- that's new from 1995. "Missing husband" is a new status. She's not a widow, which she could be, and she's not divorced and she's not married. So that's produced a problem for the women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of problem does this produce?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In a bureaucratic way, view, way, this produced the problem that if she want to start a new life, for example, if she want to get married again and she have children, and usually most of them, they don't have documents that they were married when they came because of the situation, how they came into Tuzla. So they have, according to our law, and maybe all the law in the world is the same, so they have to get married again for the missing husband, with some witnesses, usually that's mother-in-law or some cousin, so she is going with the children to get married with the missing husband, and then get divorced from the husband missing, and then she has some status, so she is divorced. And then she can get married if she wants. But some of them don't do that because of the money they will lose, that is economic problem involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean to say if a woman wants to remarry, she has to go along to the town hall and marry a missing husband; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To get the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If she doesn't have documents with her, then she can't prove that she has a husband, she has to have a witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many women from the Srebrenica survivor community that you and your organisation have dealt with have remarried since the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have three cases but they didn't remarry. That is another problem. They wanted but they didn't. I didn't finish this. Because if they do that, they will lose their income, this 300 Deutschemarks. So that's why they are -- we have -- the last cases, what we have, these women are in a big dilemma because of that. If she gets married, she will have the status of a married woman and she will lose this 300 Deutschemarks. If she don't have -- if she don't get married again, she will keep her income, but her child, she had a child with this man, will be in a difficult situation because the child is not from the official marriage. So that's bureaucratic and economic and social problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to another issue and that is the particular problems that the adult women survivors from Srebrenica have. What sort of problems do they commonly have?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the main problem that a woman from the Srebrenica survivor community has? What is the main problem that you have seen that they have?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The main problem they have with managing their life now without men, without husbands, and to keep this role of the woman that they are used to live in this traditional marriage and the family, they grow up. And with the new role they have to take over the role of the husband and to take care of the children, about the children, and they have to take care about all outside work. I mean, to get some official paper, documents, to talk with the people is sometimes hard for them. So to go out, to take these two roles, of keep the role of the women and take the role of the husband, for them is the biggest problem besides trauma in the war, what they get.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any examples you can provide of -- that illustrate this problem?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I illustrate, there is many cases of these missing husbands, but few women, they really had a big -- some big difficulties to manage their life outside of the centre in Vive Zene when they was in Vive Zene. So when they was coming in the centre and after few months they adapting to condition, what they are used to work in the centre, and then we try to help them to go out and to handle their problems, what they have -- that is, just small things about health care, documents for the health, books, more books. So they have to go outside with the public transport or to knock on some doors and to ask, to write some paper. That is the things that we are trying to help them, but not to do for them because if we do for them, so it will be the same that we take role of their husbands. So we are working on that, that finally they do that. And it was very hard for one woman to do that, and she was shocked when she went to the bus, and then she went to town. And Tuzla is very small town it's not big town. And she went in the centre for the social welfare just to ask for some paper for her children, and when she came back in the centre, it was strange for all of us when she react like she done something very big things. And she said, "Oh, I was in the bus, public bus." And for her with her 25 or 27 years, it was first time that she was in that situation, and she was really proud to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any other examples of --

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is many. There was one woman also what was for her -- I mean, these are the cases what I'm talking now what was for them very strange to do. For us it's very normal to have women do that, but for them it was -- there is in Tuzla one organisation, it's Bospor [phoen], it's name Bospor. They provide little credit, assistance for the refugee women. So they organise few women, and they get this small credit, and they can buy some sewing machine to earn some money or the cow to have some food for themselves, and that way it is organised. So when we try to explain to our women, we call it our women, Srebrenica women, that it could be also useful for them. So it is also hard for them to understand that they could work first. When you ask them that they can work, they said, "I have children." So that's explanation for them because they are used to stay at home and work. They are very responsible at home. But when you tell them you can go out and work, then she's -- it's strange for them. So with this credit and Bospor organisation, in Vive Zene we are trying to push them in some way, to help them to go in a normal life. So they -- one of them, she took the credit, and the problem was that she was waiting for the long time to finish the paper in this office of Bospor. And this -- her reaction, like previous I explain of this woman, she was very proud also, then she was waiting few times. She went to the office of Bospor and asked for the paper, and last time the girl, she was working there, she said it is not finished. But she was very strong, and before that it was strange for us because she couldn't talk almost for a few months, and then she came and she sit and she said, "I will not leave this room until you finish my paper." And it was shock for all of us, that she really show her power, that it's coming back to her, that she is very strong, and she can survive that, and she can take responsibility for this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Zecevic, and I'd like to move on to another topic and that is the particular problems that you see in the children survivors of Srebrenica in 1995. Can you describe -- can you tell me what those problems usually are?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Usually the children who was in our centre and the children we treat in the community, refugee community, and after missing -- all this what happened in Srebrenica and growing up in such a condition as you can see where they are living, they have a lot of problems with concentration, first of all in the school. And it is, besides trauma -- I will not talk about that -- but the sitting in the small room with the whole family and growing up with five years in one small room with the older people, and you don't have your place for the playing, for the learning, reading, anything, so there must be some consequences besides war and all what's happened.
