So they have a problem with the concentration, as I mentioned. And they have the problem in the family that they took some wrong roles. So like we had a few of them, and last very, very specific case is one mother, she have two girls and boy. Two girls is younger and boy is older, around 12 years, the boy. He is very, very bad in the school, very bad. All bad marks, but mother don't recognise that, and she just don't think that he is bad. The girls are always alone in our kindergarten. They take care of each other, but mother, she's talking with the boy because he is a man. So he's always in our working room where the sewing machine we have. He's with the women, all the women, other women from the group, and he controls, somehow he control his mother, what she's doing, how she's behaving. And then few times I find out that she's talking a coffee when he wake up in the morning. So he don't go downstairs in the kitchen because he's tired or whatever, but she bring the coffee to him like to his -- her husband. So she change this relation in the family, mother with the children, so she behave to him and she give him the role of the father, of the man. And when they are discussing about the money, small what they have, how they would spend, so she discuss with him, not with the girls. Not with some others, just with him. And that's with this boy a big problem because maybe he'll like it, but he's very confused with that because it's too much for him on his back to have this role of the father or the man responsibility, and he can't manage that in the school, also he have problems. He feel sometimes very nice and important because the mother ask him in front of all of us, but it's very bad in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The adolescents from this community, are they employed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The young teenagers from the Srebrenica survivor community --

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They are not employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of problems does the lack of income cause to them?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the problem what they have -- this adolescent, you mean? Adolescent, they also don't have, I always repeat, the normal life because they don't have really normal life, so they spend their times all the day in front of these houses waiting that something happen. And they don't have any possibility to work. They sometimes clean some flats around, the girls. The men, they are going in the market. Maybe you heard about Arizona. It's in a borderline of Republika Srpska and Federation. They do some black, black market or -- and then finally when they don't have anything else to do, so they get married. They get married very young in this community, in this refugee settlement. It's some solution for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on again and ask you, in your experience, from your experience in dealing with the women in the Srebrenica survivor community, what generally is their attitude to returning to their homes?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So generally all of them, they want to go back, and they would go back. But they -- deeply inside when you start to talk about that with them, so they are very afraid, very afraid about going back. And they don't have trust any more, so they lost their trust.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So they are afraid of the neighbours, maybe, former neighbours because they have very bad experience from Srebrenica and all other. And not just that they are afraid and they don't believe any more, so they are also afraid about what they will do there when they go back because usually they are from the villages, as I mentioned, as you know. So usually they have the houses with the ground; now it's destroyed. So even if you or me or whoever bring the house back in a good condition and she go back with the children, what she will do there? That's their concern. Where will be the income? Where the children will go to school?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the majority of people treated by your organisation are from the Srebrenica community, but do you also treat other victims of war trauma?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we treat, we treat them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the main difference between the victims of Srebrenica in 1995 and other victims of war trauma?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We treated -- the main difference for what we made conclusion is this missing person. I mean, that is the first and the biggest difference that start to send phenomena of missing person is -- for these women because you can't work in the process of recovery. They are stuck. They are waiting position always. They are keeping their thought that husbands will come back, that they will -- they are living somewhere. So you can't work in the hill, and they can't move any step. So they are all in this waiting position. But other people, other women we treat, they have their husbands, they know that they are killed. So they see the graves, so they finish with this mourning process, or they are in middle of the process. But with the missing person they never start this process. So that is the big, big difference for our team to work with. And also this feeling of Potocari, this collective trauma and collective guilt, it's big difference, and that's a feeling that this feeling of guilt, I mentioned it. It's -- they was all together, they was all together with the husbands and brothers, with the fathers, and they thought they are safe, and they stay, and they leave them. They thought that they leave them to go in the buses, whatever, and they feel that not so good because they -- she feel that he left behind her, that she's guilty on some way, that she didn't know that she will never see him. Maybe she will behave in different way if she know that he will stay. That's the concern. What they always have that they could do, she could do something better in the last moment. So this feeling inside them, what they have, it's very tough for them to live it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Magda Karagiannakis. Ms. Visnjic, do you have any questions to ask of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Judge Fouad Riad, but let me just remind you that we will need to have a break soon. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Zecevic, good morning. I gathered that your main problem is the rehabilitation of the women of Srebrenica? Did I -- do you think I say it rightly?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Our main problem is rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Psychological and social?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in general, how many women do you have without, without husbands now?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In our centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, the refugee settlement in general. Can you speak for the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know this information exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can just tell about our centre, in therapy centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Let us concentrate on your centre.

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is 60 women what we treat in our centre from Srebrenica from 1995, survivors from 1995 with the missing husbands; and 80 women outside of the centre in this collective settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Within these 60 missing husbands, how many are known to be dead, and how many are still in a waiting position, as you said?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are all still in the waiting position. Just one woman get a paper. She didn't see the bones, but she get the paper from Red Cross that he -- that they find the body of her husband. It was in 1997. Just one woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, how much you think these women who have not been ready to face life, because you said it was a patriarchal society and were completely sheltered, how much are they, in your opinion, capable now of starting a new life?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If they have condition, if they have condition what concern infrastructure and income without husband, they could start, all of them who passed therapy centre of Vive Zene, and they could start the normal life, so they can survive. With the condition I mean of infrastructure of income, of normal house and surrounding, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And is it being done? Is this in the process of being done, to give them this natural, normal life?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, because they have to go back. They are still in the refugee settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Their only chance is to go back, no other possibility? These refugee centres cannot be changed into permanent residences. You know, refugees all over part of the world for 50 years now.

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It could be maybe in the future, they could be -- these settlements could be arranged and in each house one family lived. It could be arranged if it will be like that, but according to the data and everything, they have to go back. So it's not planned that they will stay in refugee settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about the children, is there education going on, or are they really lost in life?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They are going on now, but most of them, all of them, they missed for at least one year of school. They will finish, but they have difficulties in learning, and they have difficulties with concentration, but they will finish the school. They have possibility near the settlements to go to school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in your opinion as a therapist, this generation can be saved?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Saved? This generation will survive, I will call it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the women?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They survived, in this moment they survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how could they go back to a normal life?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I told you, they could go back. It will never be a normal life for them like they used to live before. It will be their life, the new life, and we are trying to help them with a new structure, with their children. So they will survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just my last question. How many institutions are like yours, like Vive Zene?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia, there is just one other NGO. Medika in Zenica and Vive Zene in Tuzla; so there are just two institutions like ours, NGOs. But there is also the clinic and other governmental institutions. But Vive Zene and Medika in Zenica are just two organisations in the Federation to treat the women and children of Srebrenica and other refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are doing a great job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one or two questions and they are about the children. Is it true that most of the Srebrenica survivor families that you deal with are families of women and children without a male, without an adult male presence there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We treat just women and children without males.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So what do you think the effect of the lack of male role models, you know, fathers for children, both boys and girls, has? Is that a strong problem too, that they don't have adult working role models to model themselves after?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's not just the men who are working that's important for them. I mean, the model of a father -- a missing father is a big problem and will produce the consequences later on, and I don't know which kind. It depends on the structure of children, the structure of life, what they have now. Certainly they will have some differences than the normal family, but we could talk about that just after a few years. I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Are you able to tell, among some of these adolescents that you talked about who are growing up, the survivors, are you able to tell their attitude toward going back one day to Srebrenica? In other words, do they have any attraction toward going back, or is their only wish to get a way out into the bigger world?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the adolescents, for the young people, they don't talk about going back. They really don't talk -- their wish is just -- their dream is just to go outside, far away from Bosnia. Just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Zecevic, I have a few questions for you. You spoke about an interdisciplinary team. I should like to know who is the person who coordinates the work of that team?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The person who coordinates it is the psychotherapist. Do you need the name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the name.

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A psychotherapist for the women, and she is the coordinator of the whole psychosocial programme in the centre. She leads that team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of your work as a therapist, is there a possibility for women to talk amongst themselves without the presence of a therapist?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course there is. In the centre, they live like one family. So besides the therapist, the work with the therapist, with the doctor, social worker, they have organised their life in the centre. They have their living room; they have their dining room. They are sitting together, drinking coffee, and talking about whatever they want. So they are talking also about their problems and what's happened with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the problems that you experience in your work is the problem of missing persons. You spoke about that absence and the way it affects the women. In your opinion, what is the way in which the children and the adolescents are experiencing this absence, the absence of the missing persons from their lives?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the children and also for the adolescents, it's the same effects as for the mother, because it's a strange category for them. They are still waiting. Because they are listening to the stories from the mothers, because they are always with them, they are living together in a small room, they are always listening to the stories from the mothers. One problem I didn't mention also is that sometimes when they grow, after four or five years, when they are listening about her story, and usually she repeats that it would be better if she is dead and he is alive, so sometimes it's happened that the children take that guilt -- give that guilt again to the mother in the end when she or he is angry, and then he says, "It will be better that you are dead and father is alive." So also this transfer of the feeling of guilt is happening. So it's also the same consequences for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there any way, any possibility for these people, women in particular, women survivors of Srebrenica, to take part in the organisation of the centre?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They are living with us so they are cooking in the kitchen, they are helping our cooker. You mean in our centre? Yes. So they also have -- we have meetings, I have meetings every Friday with them, and we call it an organisational meeting. So they have their duties but also their rights. So that is part of what we are trying to give them, from the patriarchal structure, to teach them that they have some rights but they have to ask for the rights. We will not give them by ourselves; they have to ask for the rights. So they have obligations, they have duties, but they have also their rights. That is part of the healing process. Besides the professional work of trauma and recovery and all kinds of therapy they get, this part of the structuring of their life, we consider very important for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, there is work to be done so that there can be a change of standards, a change of cultural perceptions in their lives. Do you sometimes invite other people, people coming from other cultures, or women who have different circumstances, who live alone, for example, who can come and talk to your women about their situation?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have a part of the psychotherapy centre -- what we have is we have one small social project in the school Dokanje, in the surroundings of Tuzla, and that is where different people, a category of people, are living; that is, domicile people, refugees, and returnees. That is three different nations: Muslim people, Croats, and Serbs. So we have for Bajram, that's -- you know what Bajram is. The women from the centre of Vive Zene, we invite them to this and they have like a party. It's not a party but they are sitting together. So we call that project social recovery and rebuilding the trust in these groups. So we make -- and we are working on this also in the refugee community, on integration. In the local community, even it is very hard, and we are doing that. We are trying to do the best from our side, but it's not -- in a community of refugees, it's harder because they are isolated groups. But these women from the centre, they have contact with the project in Dokanje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I see that my colleague Judge Fouad Riad has another question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Are there any women among the ones you have who are not Muslims who are married to Muslims and are left behind?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We had in -- but it's not a Srebrenica woman. I mean, in the centre we had in 1994 one woman from Gradacac and she was married to a Muslim. He was killed. She was in our centre in the first group, in 1994, with other Muslim women. She was the only one because all the refugees that were coming into Tuzla, it was mostly women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The children from these marriages, how are they considered?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean how they are treated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How they are treated, and to whom do they belong?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They belong to the mother because they were with the mother in our centre. Two boys, they were with their mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they are considered -- I mean, she was a Serb or a Croat? Whatever. The children are considered as belonging to the mother, or they are following the father's steps?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The children stay with the mother. The mother raised them. So I don't have a clear explanation for that because that is a big problem. You asked if they are Croats or Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How are they treated? What future do they have?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They have a future the same, like all other children in Bosnia who don't have a father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but which community is accepting them?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The community of Tuzla town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is there a new community where there is no discrimination?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Tuzla there is no discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you think that will be the future of this part of the world, no discrimination?

utterances.speaker: JASNA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think in Tuzla -- especially in Tuzla it is a multicultural society. Others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Jasna Zecevic. Thank you for coming, and we wish you a great deal of success in your work. I think that you have a very important task to perform, you and other persons like you who are willing to work in this area, which is extremely important for providing living conditions for victims who have suffered, whoever they may be. I'm talking about all victims of all conflicts. So we wish you success in your work and a happy journey to your place of residence where there are many people who need you. Ms. Magda, I think there are some documents to be tendered into evidence. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender the video, which was Exhibit 386, and the photo, which was Exhibit 390, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these exhibits have been admitted into evidence. Before we adjourn for a break, do we have other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we have no other witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: We have one witness for tomorrow, the last witness for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we will meet again tomorrow at 9.30. I wish you a pleasant afternoon, and bon voyage to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
